questions.q: How does alerting differ from the dashboard-based monitoring covered in Lesson 22?
options: An alert condition is evaluated continuously and fires automatically, instead of requiring a human to be actively watching a dashboard
Alerting replaces the need for any dashboard or monitoring numbers
Alerting only works if someone manually refreshes a page every minute
Alerting and dashboard monitoring are identical in every respect
questions.explain: Dashboards require someone to be looking at the right moment; alerting removes that dependency by firing automatically when a condition is true.

questions.q: Why can't an alerting system simply be told to "alert me if something anomalous happens"?
options: That instruction isn't a condition a system can evaluate -- it has to be broken into specific, checkable trigger types
Alerting systems can evaluate vague instructions just as well as specific ones
Anomalous activity never actually occurs on-chain
Alert trigger types are limited to exactly one type: failed transactions
questions.explain: Real alerting platforms require specific trigger types -- like a failed transaction or an unexpected caller -- because a system can't evaluate a vague condition.

questions.q: Why does keeping every active alert rule visible in one dashboard matter, rather than in individual team members' personal scripts?
options: It means the question "are we watching for X?" has an answer anyone on the team can check, not just the person who set the rule up
It has no practical benefit over scattered personal scripts
It automatically fixes any bugs in the underlying smart contract
It prevents the team from ever needing to update a rule
questions.explain: Rules that live only in one person's private script aren't reliable team-wide monitoring -- they depend on that one person remembering to run them.

questions.q: What happens when an alert is calibrated too broadly, firing on routine activity?
options: The team tends to start ignoring it within a short time, making it effectively useless -- alert fatigue
It becomes more useful the more often it fires, regardless of relevance
The alerting platform automatically narrows it for you
It has no negative effect on how the team responds to future alerts
questions.explain: An alert that fires on routine, non-actionable activity trains the team to ignore it -- a muted channel is worse than no alert at all.

questions.q: What does this lesson say a useful alert notification should include to be immediately actionable?
options: The transaction hash, the network, and a direct link back to the dashboard
Only the words "something happened" with no further detail
The full Solidity source code of the contract involved
A request for the recipient to guess which contract triggered it
questions.explain: A specific transaction hash, network, and dashboard link let the recipient start investigating immediately instead of hunting for context.
